## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pārājika 3, titled *Manussaviggaha*, sets forth the third rule of defeat concerning the intentional deprivation of human life (*sañcicca manussaviggahaṁ jīvitā voropeyya*), an offence entailing expulsion from the Saṅgha [Collins 2001; Schmithausen 1991]. The text defines the status of one who incurs defeat with the simile of a massive rock split in two that cannot be put back together (*seyyathāpi nāma puthusilā dvedhā bhinnā appaṭisandhikā hoti*) [Clarke 2009]. In Buddhist monastic law, killing a human being is treated as an infraction far more severe than taking animal life, which is governed separately under Pācittiya 61 [Gethin 2004; Schmithausen 1991; Schmithausen 2009].

The rule's origin narrative recounts an incident where monks cultivating the meditation on the unattractiveness of the body (*asubha*) developed extreme disgust with their physical existence, leading them either to commit suicide or to solicit others to end their lives; in response, the Buddha instituted the prohibition against homicide and assisted suicide, and subsequently taught the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) [Rosen 1959]. The canonical rule is accompanied by extensive casuistry addressing varied circumstances and modes of killing, incitement to suicide, and mitigating factors [Gethin 2004; Rosen 1959].

The rule possesses full parallels across the Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅgas and Prātimokṣa traditions of the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsaṅghika, and Dharmaguptaka lineages preserved in Sanskrit fragments, Chinese, and Tibetan, as well as the Pali Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga and Parivāra [Rosen 1959]. The narrative's discourse on mindfulness of breathing corresponds to Sutta Piṭaka parallels in the Ānāpāna Saṁyutta (SN 54.1), the Ānāpānassati Sutta (MN 118), and SĀ 803. Algorithmic text-reuse data from DharmaNexus confirms a close textual match with SN 54 (0.98 similarity over §1.2.12–1.3.6), recurring structural formulas shared with other *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa* texts, and cross-linguistic alignments with Sanskrit vastus and the Tibetan *Vinayavibhaṅga* [DharmaNexus].
